\chapter{-mente --- With No Upper Limit}
\label{ch:friend-mente}
\hlchaptermodality{25}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can build an adverb from any adjective, and say why the adjective goes feminine first.}

Complete ES-C56-mente: build rapidamente, explain the feminine step, and say what the word literally means.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[-mente]{-mente — with no upper limit}

\label{lesson:ES-C56-mente}



\begin{quote}
Two endings so far, and each was worth a fixed number of words. This one has \textbf{no number}, because you can make it yourself.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: -mente is -ly}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{Spanish \emph{-mente} is English \emph{-ly}.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{rápidamente} $\to$ rapidly · \emph{claramente} $\to$ clearly · \emph{perfectamente} $\to$ perfectly · \emph{naturalmente} $\to$ naturally
\end{quote}

And unlike the last two endings, this one is a \textbf{machine} rather than a list: take an adjective, put it in its \textbf{feminine} form, add \emph{-mente}.

\begin{quote}
\emph{rápido} $\to$ \emph{rápida} $\to$ \textbf{rápidamente} \emph{claro} $\to$ \emph{clara} $\to$ \textbf{claramente}
\end{quote}

That feminine step looks arbitrary and is not — the next section says why. But the practical effect is that every adjective you ever learn comes with a free adverb, which is why this ending has no count attached. Its reach is however many adjectives you end up knowing.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{-mente} is not an ending at all, historically. It is the Latin noun \textbf{mente}, \textquotedblleft{}with a mind\textquotedblright{} — and \emph{mente} is \textbf{feminine}, which is the whole explanation for that feminine adjective.

Latin said \emph{clārā mente}, \textquotedblleft{}with a clear mind,\textquotedblright{} and the adjective agreed with the noun because that is what adjectives do. Then the phrase fused, the noun stopped being a noun, and the agreement was left behind as a rule nobody could explain any more.

So \emph{rápidamente} is, at the bottom, \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}with a rapid mind.\textquotedblright{}} Every Spanish adverb in \emph{-mente} is quietly a phrase about somebody's state of mind.

English does exactly the same thing with a different body part. \textbf{-ly} is Old English \emph{-līce}, from \emph{līc}, \textquotedblleft{}body, form\textquotedblright{} — so \emph{clearly} is \textquotedblleft{}in a clear form.\textquotedblright{} Two languages, two fused nouns, the same idea.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}rápido, rápida, rápidamente\textquotedblright{} — watch the feminine step
  \item \textquotedblleft{}claramente\textquotedblright{} and hear \textquotedblleft{}with a clear mind\textquotedblright{} underneath it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
English \emph{-ly} becomes? (\emph{\textbf{-mente}}.) What do you do to the adjective first? (Make it \textbf{feminine}.) And why? (Because \emph{\textbf{mente}} was a \textbf{feminine noun} meaning \emph{mind}.) Next: the three of them together.
\end{tcolorbox}
